Topic: KV cache compression and eviction policies for long-context transformer serving

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-157)
response:
The central question is: given that storing full KV caches for long-context inference is prohibitively expensive (a single 128k-token request with a 70B model can require tens of GBs of DRAM per sequence), how do you decide which keys and values to keep, evict, or compress without meaningfully degrading output quality? The key concepts are the KV cache itself (the materialized attention keys and values for all past tokens, stored to avoid recomputation), eviction policies (rules for which tokens to drop — recency-based, attention-score-based, or learned), and compression schemes (quantizing KV tensors to INT4/INT8, low-rank approximation, or merging similar tokens into summary vectors). The expert-level worry that beginners miss is policy-model coupling: an eviction heuristic calibrated on one architecture or task can be catastrophically wrong on another, because what makes a token's KV entry "safe to drop" depends on the specific attention patterns the model learned — sparse retrieval heads behave nothing like dense summarization heads, and a single policy applied uniformly across all heads is almost certainly wrong for at least some of them. A second non-obvious concern is error accumulation under generation: compression artifacts that look negligible on perplexity benchmarks can compound during autoregressive decoding because each generated token is conditioned on the degraded cache, shifting the distribution in ways that only manifest dozens of tokens later. Experts also track prefill/decode asymmetry — compression decisions made during prefill (when the full prompt is known) admit very different algorithms than online eviction during decode (where you can't see future tokens), and most academic benchmarks conflate the two.

For a given eviction policy — say, dropping tokens with the lowest cumulative attention scores — what is the concrete failure mode when that policy encounters a "retrieval" query whose answer token appeared only once, early in a 100k-token document?

The failure is straightforward but brutal: a token that appears once early in the document accumulates almost no attention weight during the prefill pass over the intervening 90k+ tokens of irrelevant context, so a cumulative-score eviction policy like H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle, Zhang et al. 2023) ranks it near the bottom and evicts it — permanently, since most serving systems make eviction decisions without lookahead. When the query arrives at decode time, the model issues high-weight attention toward the now-absent KV entry, but the cache returns vectors from whatever survived eviction (often recent tokens, due to the well-documented "recency sink" bias), so the model is effectively confabulating an answer from wrong context. H2O reported strong average-case perplexity preservation but the evaluation was on tasks like language modeling and summarization, not needle-in-a-haystack retrieval — the distributional mismatch between benchmark and deployment is exactly the trap. SnapKV (Li et al. 2024) specifically diagnosed this by measuring per-task eviction sensitivity and found that single-fact retrieval tasks degraded sharply at cache budgets where summarization tasks were nearly unaffected, with accuracy dropping from ~90% to under 40% at 10% cache retention on NIAH benchmarks. The deeper issue is that cumulative attention scores are a proxy for past relevance, not future query relevance — a token that no head has attended to yet is not the same as a token that no head will attend to, and early-document facts are structurally disadvantaged by the causal left-to-right accumulation dynamic.

The cleanest architectural signal is to train the model to emit explicit "importance tokens" or use a dedicated sentinel head whose attention weights during prefill serve as a retention score — this is the intuition behind CAKE (Cache-Aware Knowledge Encoding, 2024) and related work that fine-tunes models to be eviction-aware, so the model itself learns to concentrate attention on tokens it will need later. A serving-system approach that requires no retraining is speculative prefill scoring: run a cheap auxiliary model (a 1-2B parameter probe, or even a single transformer layer distilled from the full model) over the document to produce saliency estimates before the full prefill, then use those scores to set per-token protection flags — the cost is one cheap forward pass amortized over what may be thousands of decode steps. A third signal comes from retrieval-augmented structure: if the serving system knows the document was chunked for RAG, chunk-boundary tokens and BM25-salient spans can be pinned unconditionally, exploiting external document structure that the model's attention pattern can't see during a single-pass prefill. Oracle experiments in the SnapKV paper showed that if you protect even the top 5% of tokens by ground-truth future attention weight, retrieval accuracy is nearly fully recovered — meaning the problem is not cache size but signal quality, and a good proxy score is sufficient. The fundamental tension is that any probe or auxiliary model introduces latency and memory overhead at prefill, which is already the bottleneck for long-context serving, so the practical constraint is that your importance estimator must be faster than the attention computation it is trying to guide — roughly, it needs to run in under 10-15% of full prefill time to be deployable.

The protection policy ideally needs to become a dynamic set that is re-scored after each query-response pair, promoting tokens newly relevant to the emerging conversation thread and demoting tokens whose queries have been answered — but this requires either re-prefilling the entire document (prohibitively expensive) or maintaining a secondary index over KV entries that can be re-ranked without recomputation. The hardest part is that eviction is typically irreversible: once a KV entry is dropped to free DRAM, recovering it means recomputing attention over the original tokens, which requires storing the raw token IDs and re-running prefill for the evicted span — SGLang and vLLM both support prefix caching that partially mitigates this for shared prefixes, but evicted mid-document tokens have no such reuse path. A second difficulty is query intent ambiguity: the system doesn't know at turn 1 whether the user's turn-2 query will pivot to a different section of the document or drill deeper into the same one, so any re-scoring must hedge across plausible future queries, which is essentially a distribution estimation problem with a sample size of one. CacheBlend (2024) attacked a related problem by selectively recomputing KV entries for tokens that appear in multiple documents, showing that partial recomputation of ~10-15% of tokens recovers most accuracy — suggesting that a tiered policy (pin critical tokens, recompute on-demand for newly relevant ones, evict the rest) is architecturally feasible but requires the serving system to track token provenance and recomputation cost per span. The deepest hardness is memory fragmentation: a dynamic protection policy that promotes and demotes tokens across turns creates non-contiguous live sets in the KV cache, and vLLM's PagedAttention-style block allocator was designed for prefix-structured sharing, not arbitrary mid-sequence resurrection, so dynamic re-pinning forces either large internal fragmentation or expensive block remapping that can itself become a throughput bottleneck.

subject: KV cache compression and eviction policies for long-context transformer serving
prompt:
Given that recomputing evicted tokens is sometimes necessary, what is the exact break-even condition — in terms of token count, model size, and hardware arithmetic intensity — at which recomputation is cheaper than the memory bandwidth cost of retaining and reading those KV entries throughout the session?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-161)
response:
The break-even condition is determined by comparing two costs: recomputation cost (FLOPs to rerun attention over N evicted tokens, paid once) versus retention cost (memory bandwidth to read those N KV entries on every decode step, paid T times where T is remaining decode steps). For a model with H attention heads, head dimension D, and L layers, storing N tokens costs 2·N·H·D·L·sizeof(dtype) bytes — for Llama-3 70B in FP16 that's roughly 320·N KB per layer, or ~80GB for 10k tokens across all layers — and on an A100 with 2TB/s HBM bandwidth, reading that cache costs ~40ms per decode step at full occupancy. Recomputation cost for N tokens scales as O(N²) in attention FLOPs (for the evicted span attending to itself) plus O(N·S) for attending to the surviving context of length S, and on an A100 at ~300 TFLOPS BF16, recomputing 1k tokens through 80 layers of Llama-3 70B takes roughly 200-400ms — meaning recomputation breaks even against retention if the evicted tokens would otherwise be read for more than ~5-10 additional decode steps. The key non-obvious factor is arithmetic intensity of the recomputation kernel: prefill is compute-bound (high arithmetic intensity, good GPU utilization) while decode KV reads are memory-bound (low arithmetic intensity, bandwidth-limited), so the hardware efficiency ratio strongly favors recomputation on compute-dense accelerators — this is why FlashAttention's authors noted that recomputation during backprop is often faster than storing activations, an analogy that carries directly to inference. In practice the break-even sits around N=500-2000 tokens for sessions longer than 50-100 decode steps on current H100/A100 hardware, but shifts dramatically with quantization: INT4 KV cache cuts retention bandwidth cost by 4x, pushing break-even toward recomputation being favorable only for very short remaining sessions or very large evicted spans.

The mechanism turns on the dynamic range of the key vectors that each head type produces: vertical heads (which attend to a small set of globally important tokens — sink tokens, punctuation, special tokens) produce key vectors with extremely high variance across the sequence, because the "target" tokens have keys that are outlier-magnitude relative to the rest, and INT4 quantization with a per-tensor or even per-token scale is forced to allocate its 16 bins across that full dynamic range, leaving only 1-2 bins of resolution for the majority of non-sink keys. Diagonal heads, by contrast, attend locally and produce key vectors whose magnitudes are relatively uniform across the sequence window, so the same 16 INT4 bins are distributed across a much narrower range and quantization error per entry is proportionally smaller. The consequence for vertical heads is that after quantization, the softmax attention scores for sink tokens become imprecise enough that the head occasionally "misses" the sink and redistributes weight to neighboring tokens — KVQuant (Hooper et al. 2024) measured this directly, finding that vertical heads showed 3-5x higher perplexity degradation per layer under INT4 versus diagonal heads at equivalent bit budgets, and attributed it specifically to key outlier magnitude asymmetry. The compounding across layers occurs because transformer residual streams accumulate: a vertical head in layer 10 that slightly mis-attends to a sink token produces a subtly corrupted residual, which shifts the key/value distributions in layer 11, making that layer's quantization error correlated with (and amplified by) the previous error rather than independent. QuIP# and AQLM both address this by using incoherence preprocessing (random orthogonal rotation of key matrices before quantization) to spread outlier energy across all dimensions, reducing per-channel dynamic range at the cost of a matrix multiply before each attention operation — this recovers most of the vertical head degradation but adds ~5-8% latency overhead per layer.

Since incoherence preprocessing rotates key matrices to suppress outliers, but the rotation must be applied consistently at both cache-write time and query-time, what happens to this scheme under speculative decoding where draft and target models may have different rotation matrices or quantization configurations?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-163)
response:
In standard speculative decoding the draft model generates K tokens whose KV entries are written into a shared cache, and the target model then verifies them in a single parallel forward pass — if draft and target use different rotation matrices R_draft and R_target, the target model's query vectors are rotated by R_target but the cached keys were written under R_draft, so the attention scores compute q·R_target·(R_draft·k)^T instead of q·k^T, injecting a fixed linear distortion (R_target·R_draft^T) into every attention score for draft-generated tokens. This is not a small perturbation: random orthogonal matrices are maximally incoherent by design, so R_target·R_draft^T is itself a near-random rotation, and the resulting attention score corruption is severe enough to invalidate verification — the target model will reject nearly all draft tokens not because they are wrong but because the KV geometry is incompatible, collapsing speculative decoding's acceptance rate toward zero. The practical constraint this imposes is that any system using incoherence-preprocessed quantized KV caches must enforce a single shared rotation matrix across all models that touch the same cache, which means draft and target must either use identical R (requiring coordination at model export time) or the draft must write unrotated keys that the target rotates on read — adding a matrix multiply per attention layer per draft token at verification time, partially eating the latency gains speculative decoding was meant to provide. This problem is not yet cleanly solved in production systems; vLLM's speculative decoding implementation as of early 2025 sidesteps it by not supporting KV quantization on draft model caches, effectively forfeiting compression on the draft's contribution. A deeper issue is that even if rotation matrices are shared, draft and target models typically have different weight distributions and may require different per-channel quantization scales, meaning the same INT4 grid that is well-matched to the target's key distribution may be poorly matched to the draft's — EAGLE-2's architecture partially mitigates this by making the draft model a shallow adapter on the target's own hidden states, ensuring KV distributions stay close enough that a shared quantization config is approximately valid.

The redundancy is real but partial: EAGLE-2's draft model takes the target's hidden states as input, so its key and value projections are functions of representations the target has already computed — but because the draft has its own W_K and W_V projection matrices (even if shallow), the resulting KV tensors are not identical to the target's and cannot be directly substituted. However, the mutual information between draft and target KV entries is very high, which means you could in principle store only the target's KV entries in DRAM and reconstruct the draft's on-the-fly by applying the draft's lightweight projection to the target's cached hidden states — this costs one small matrix multiply per layer per token at draft-step time, but avoids writing a second full KV cache to DRAM, which for a 70B target with a 1B EAGLE draft saves roughly 1.4% of total cache memory (small, but meaningful at scale). The catch is that EAGLE-2 does not cache the target's intermediate hidden states by default — only the KV entries — so reconstructing draft KVs from target hiddens would require either also caching hidden states (doubling memory for those layers) or recomputing them, and hidden states are larger than KV entries for typical head configurations, making this trade negative in most regimes. Medusa and related multi-head draft architectures face the same issue but handle it differently: their draft heads operate directly on the final hidden state of the last target layer, which is already resident in the forward pass compute graph, so within a single forward pass the draft heads are genuinely zero-extra-memory — but across decode steps the last-layer hidden state is not cached, so inter-step reuse still requires storing something. The most promising exploit of this redundancy is not eliminating draft KV writes entirely but using the target's KV entries as a compressed basis for the draft's, expressing the draft's keys as a low-rank correction to the target's keys (ΔK = draft_K - target_K, which empirically has much lower rank than either alone) — this delta compression could reduce draft cache size by 60-80% in early experiments analogous to those in LoRA-inspired KV compression work (Memserve, 2024), though no production system has shipped this specific optimization yet.
